claim: High-throughput vertebrate animal model systems for the study of patient-specific biology and new therapeutic approaches for aggressive brain tumors are currently lacking.
source: High-throughput vertebrate animal model systems for the study of patient-specific biology and new therapeutic approaches for aggressive brain tumors are currently lacking, and new approaches are urgently needed.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field presented in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Expression of activated human EGFRvIII and PI3KCAH1047R under the control of the radial glial-specific promoter her4.1 in syngeneic tp53 loss-of-function mutant zebrafish results in robust tumor formation prior to 45 days of life.
source: Therefore, to build a patient-relevant in vivo model of human glioblastoma, we expressed common oncogenic variants including activated human EGFRvIII and PI3KCAH1047R under the control of the radial glial-specific promoter her4.1 in syngeneic tp53 loss-of-function mutant zebrafish. Robust tumor formation was observed prior to 45 days of life
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section with data showing tumor formation.

claim: p53EPS tumors have a gene expression signature similar to human glioblastoma of the mesenchymal subtype.
source: tumors had a gene expression signature similar to human glioblastoma of the mesenchymal subtype, with a strong inflammatory component.
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing zebrafish tumor expression data to published human glioblastoma subtype signatures.

claim: p53EPS tumors have a strong inflammatory component.
source: tumors had a gene expression signature similar to human glioblastoma of the mesenchymal subtype, with a strong inflammatory component.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis and GSEA showing enrichment for inflammatory pathways.

claim: Within early stage tumor lesions, phagocytic cells infiltrate the tumor microenvironment.
source: Within early stage tumor lesions, and in an in vivo and endogenous tumor microenvironment, we visualized infiltration of phagocytic cells
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing neutral red-positive cells and mpeg1.1:EGFP+ cells in tumor lesions.

claim: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages internalize tumor cells in early stage tumor lesions.
source: as well as internalization of tumor cells by mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages, suggesting negative regulatory pressure by pro-inflammatory cell types on tumor growth at early stages of glioblastoma initiation.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging showing mScarlet+ punctae within mpeg1.1:EGFP+ cells.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cell types exert negative regulatory pressure on tumor growth at early stages of glioblastoma initiation.
source: suggesting negative regulatory pressure by pro-inflammatory cell types on tumor growth at early stages of glioblastoma initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of tumor cell internalization by phagocytes and supported by functional experiments showing increased tumor formation when inflammatory pathways are disrupted.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene targeting of irf7 leads to increased tumor formation in the primary context.
source: Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene targeting of master inflammatory transcription factors irf7 or irf8 led to increased tumor formation in the primary context
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 65% tumor incidence with irf7 targeting compared to 20% in controls.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene targeting of irf8 leads to increased tumor formation in the primary context.
source: Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene targeting of master inflammatory transcription factors irf7 or irf8 led to increased tumor formation in the primary context
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 42% tumor incidence with irf8 targeting compared to 20% in controls.

claim: Suppression of phagocyte activity leads to enhanced tumor cell engraftment following transplantation into immune-competent zebrafish hosts.
source: while suppression of phagocyte activity led to enhanced tumor cell engraftment following transplantation into otherwise immune-competent zebrafish hosts.
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments using Clodronate liposomes and irf8 knockdown hosts showing increased engraftment rates.

claim: Glioblastoma represents about 50% of all primary brain malignancies in adults.
source: New approaches that reflect patient genetics and physiology have the potential to aid in improving therapeutic strategies for individuals with malignant brain tumors like glioblastoma, which represents about 50% of all primary brain malignancies in adults (Ostrom et al., 2017; Torp et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most patients with glioblastoma eventually relapse and have a median survival rate of less than 15 months despite intensive treatments including surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.
source: Despite intensive treatments including surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy (temozolomide), most patients with glioblastoma eventually relapse and have a median survival rate of less than 15 months (Aldape et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Three major subtypes of glioblastoma have been classified: proneural, classical, and mesenchymal.
source: Molecular heterogeneity has been important for the classification of three major subtypes of glioblastoma including proneural, classical, and mesenchymal (Brennan et al., 2013; Torp et al., 2022; Verhaak and Valk, 2010; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: 90% of glioblastoma tumors display alterations in core signaling factors involved in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/RAS/PI3K pathway signaling.
source: In general, 90% of glioblastoma tumors display alterations in core signaling factors involved in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/RAS/PI3K pathway signaling (Brennan et al., 2013; McLendon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Amplifications and/or activating mutations in EGFR are found in >50% of glioblastomas.
source: While activating mutations in RAS proteins are rarely found in the clinic, loss of the negative regulator NF1 is common, as well as amplifications and/or activating mutations in various RAS pathway proteins including epidermal growth factors receptor (EGFR), which are found in >50% of glioblastomas (Brennan et al., 2013; Hoogstrate et al., 2022; McLendon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The TP53 tumor suppressor pathway is altered in 84% of glioblastoma patients and 94% of cell lines.
source: Furthermore, the TP53 tumor suppressor pathway is altered in 84% of globlastoma patients and 94% of cell lines, with TP53 loss implicated in tumor cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and stemness (Brennan et al., 2013; McLendon et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Single pathway mutations are generally insufficient to transform normal brain tissues, and multiple mutations are required for glioma formation.
source: Importantly, single pathway mutations are generally insufficient to transform normal brain tissues, and multiple mutations are required for glioma formation (Chen et al., 2018; Haddad et al., 2021; Holland et al., 2013; Takke et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Co-injection of linearized her4.1:EGFRvIII + her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R + her4.1:mScarlet transgenes into syngeneic tp53-/- mutant embryos at the one-cell stage led to visible mScarlet-positive brain lesions in the anterior CNS at 15 days post fertilization.
source: Co-injection of linearized her4.1:EGFRvIII + her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R + her4.1:mScarlet transgenes into syngeneic (CG1) tp53-/- mutant embryos at the one-cell stage led to broad transient mScarlet expression for 5–6 days followed by rare mosaic expression in the anterior CNS (henceforth referred to as p53EPS, Figure 1A), as expected from a transient mosaic injection strategy used to express stable concatemers of DNA vectors (Langenau et al., 2008). At 15 days post fertilization (dpf), this transgene combination led to visible mScarlet-positive brain lesions in the anterior CNS of live zebrafish (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The p53EPS combination resulted in a maximum incidence of approximately 15–20% affected zebrafish by 45 dpf.
source: Injections of single linearized vector and vector combinations resulted in a maximum incidence of approximately 15–20% affected zebrafish induced by the p53EPS combination, by 45 dpf (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 27.5% of p53EPS tumors arose in the telencephalon and diencephalon regions.
source: Intertumoral variability was observed among p53EPS mosaic-injected zebrafish, with tumors of variable size arising in different brain regions including the telencephalon and diencephalon regions (8/29=27.5%, from three independent tumor screens)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of tumor locations across multiple experiments.

claim: 72.5% of p53EPS tumors arose in the optic tectum/mesencephalon region.
source: and the optic tectum/mesencephalon region (21/29=72.5%, from three independent tumor screens) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of tumor locations across multiple experiments.

claim: 100% of p53EPS brain masses at 30–40 dpf expressed EGFP when co-injected with linearized gfap:EGFP.
source: To further define the tissue of origin of zebrafish p53EPS CNS lesions, we co-injected linearized gfap:EGFP (Don et al., 2017) and visualized EGFP expression in 100% of brain masses at 30–40 dpf (Figure 1A and B), supporting glial identity and a novel in vivo model of malignant glioma.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data.

claim: p53EPS cells are oncogenically transformed and capable of malignant growth in vivo.
source: At approximately 18 days post-transplant (18 dpt, or 20 dpf), we screened for mScarlet+ fluorescence and visualized her4.1+/gfap+ tumor cell outgrowth in 16–25% of transplanted hosts (n=3 independent screens, Figure 1E and F), supporting oncogenic transformation and malignant growth in vivo of p53EPS cells.
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments showing tumor growth in recipient animals.

claim: p53EPS tumors display highly aggressive and proliferative characteristics with a heterogenous mix of different malignant cell types.
source: We performed serial sectioning of uninjected control and primary p53EPS zebrafish brains and performed histological characterizations, which revealed highly aggressive and proliferative tumors in p53EPS consisting of a heterogenous mix of different malignant cell types, compared to normal brains (Figure 1H–O, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: p53EPS tumors contain one major cell type with a round granular-like morphology with a high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio.
source: One major cell type displayed a round granular-like morphology with a high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio, while a second cell type found within the same tumor masses displayed a flattened and elongated morphology (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in the figures.

claim: p53EPS tumors contain a second cell type with a flattened and elongated morphology.
source: One major cell type displayed a round granular-like morphology with a high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio, while a second cell type found within the same tumor masses displayed a flattened and elongated morphology (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in the figures.

claim: p53EPS tumors display clean margins without invasive boundaries, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation in general.
source: In general, tumors displayed clean margins without invasive boundaries, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation; however, a few instances of cell migration along vasculature were detected.
evidence: This is based on histological characterization of tumor sections.

claim: Certain p53EPS tumors display embryonal features including rosette-type structures and a high mitotic index.
source: Certain p53EPS tumors displayed embryonal features including rosette-type structures and a high mitotic index, overlapping histological features with glioblastoma with primitive neuronal component (Suwala et al., 2021)
evidence: This is based on histological observations and comparison to published literature.

claim: p53EPS tumor lesions show increased p-ERK staining compared to normal brains.
source: Compared to normal brains, we found increased p-ERK and p-AKT staining within tumor lesions, consistent with elevated MAPK and AKT activation driving malignant transformation (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining and quantification shown in Figure 1.

claim: p53EPS tumor lesions show increased p-AKT staining compared to normal brains.
source: Compared to normal brains, we found increased p-ERK and p-AKT staining within tumor lesions, consistent with elevated MAPK and AKT activation driving malignant transformation (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining and quantification shown in Figure 1.

claim: Co-injection of linearized her4.1:KRASG12D + her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R + her4.1:EGFP into tp53-/- embryos results in tumor onset and penetrance comparable to p53EPS at 15–20 dpf.
source: To further validate effects of relevant downstream signaling pathway activation, we also co-injected linearized her4.1:KRASG12D + her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R + her4.1:EGFP into tp53-/- embryos (p53KPG). At 15–20 dpf, we visualized tumor onset and penetrance comparable to p53EPS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: MAPK/AKT pathway activation plays a dominant role in driving tumor formation downstream of RTK signaling.
source: suggesting a dominant role for MAPK/AKT pathway activation downstream of RTK signaling in driving tumor formation, and a flexible oncogenic strategy for inducing robust brain tumor formation in zebrafish.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable tumor formation observed with both EGFRvIII and KRASG12D drivers when combined with PI3KCAH1047R.

claim: Control-injected zebrafish brains cluster together and apart from p53EPS and p53KPS tumor brains in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: Using hierarchical clustering on normalized gene expression, our tumor-free control samples clustered together and apart from p53EPS and p53KPS tumor brains, which displayed a recognizable level of transcriptional variability across principal components (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: p53EPS and p53KPS samples fail to cluster according to oncogenic drivers.
source: Interestingly, p53EPS and p53KPS samples failed to cluster according to oncogenic drivers (Figure 2A), suggesting molecular similarities as well as inter-tumor heterogeneity reflecting differences in tumor location, size, and contribution of tumor cells to total sample inputs.
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 236 genes are significantly upregulated in p53EPS tumor brains compared to control-injected brains.
source: Using differential gene expression analysis, we identified a conserved set of differentially expressed (DE) genes in p53EPS tumor brains, with 236 significantly upregulated and 28 downregulated genes, compared to control-injected brains at 20–30 dpf (2>log2foldChange>–2, adjusted p-value<0.05, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: 28 genes are significantly downregulated in p53EPS tumor brains compared to control-injected brains.
source: Using differential gene expression analysis, we identified a conserved set of differentially expressed (DE) genes in p53EPS tumor brains, with 236 significantly upregulated and 28 downregulated genes, compared to control-injected brains at 20–30 dpf (2>log2foldChange>–2, adjusted p-value<0.05, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: p53EPS zebrafish model shows significant enrichment for the mesenchymal subtype of human glioblastoma.
source: Among these gene sets, we found a significant enrichment for the mesenchymal subtype of human glioblastoma in p53EPS DE genes (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3; McLendon et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing zebrafish tumor expression to published human glioblastoma subtype signatures.

claim: No significant enrichment was found for other glioblastoma or medulloblastoma subtypes in p53EPS samples.
source: In contrast, while certain genes for other glioblastoma and/or medulloblastoma subtypes were upregulated in p53EPS samples, no significant enrichment was found for these specific gene expression signatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3; Cavalli et al., 2017; McLendon et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis results shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: 7 of the top 13 enriched Hallmark gene sets in p53EPS relate to inflammation or inflammatory signaling pathways.
source: Interestingly, 7 of the top 13 enriched gene sets identified (NOM p-value<0.05) related to inflammation or inflammatory signaling pathways, including the interferon gamma response, TNFA signaling, the interferon alpha response, and Jak/STAT3 signaling (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 4)
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of Hallmark pathways.

claim: p53EPS tumors show enrichment for gene expression signatures related to RAS signaling, hypoxia, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions.
source: Additional pathway signatures included those related to RAS signaling, hypoxia, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions (Supplementary file 4), suggesting on-target oncogenic pathway activation, hypoxia, and invasive properties, consistent with aggressive glioblastoma (Majc et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis and comparison to published literature on glioblastoma characteristics.

claim: Both p53EPS tumor cells and stromal cells show increased immune cell and inflammatory gene expression compared to control whole brain tissue.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased immune cell and inflammatory gene expression in both p53EPS tumor and stromal cell fractions compared to control unaffected whole brain tissue, including transcripts associated with myeloid cell types (mpeg1, irf7, irf8), lymphoid progenitor and specific subtype regulators (rag1, rag2, lck), stat1a/b, fas cell surface death receptor, and Toll-like receptor 4b (tlr4bb), among other genes involved in immune responses (adjusted p-value<0.0001, Figure 2E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing analysis of FACS-sorted cell populations.

claim: p53EPS tumors show co-expression of her4.1:mScarlet and rag2:EGFP.
source: Interestingly, we observed co-expression of her4.1:mScarlet/rag2:EGFP and her4.1:mScarlet/mpeg1.1:EGFP in p53EPS tumors (Figure 2F–I), suggesting promoter activity at certain immune-associated genes within established p53EPS tumor cells in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging of tumors with co-injected reporter constructs.

claim: p53EPS tumors show co-expression of her4.1:mScarlet and mpeg1.1:EGFP.
source: Interestingly, we observed co-expression of her4.1:mScarlet/rag2:EGFP and her4.1:mScarlet/mpeg1.1:EGFP in p53EPS tumors (Figure 2F–I), suggesting promoter activity at certain immune-associated genes within established p53EPS tumor cells in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging of tumors with co-injected reporter constructs.

claim: Neutral red-positive phagocyte foci are enriched in regions of her4.1:mScarlet+ fluorescent intensity at 10 dpf.
source: At 10 dpf, we observed enrichment of neutral red-positive foci in regions of her4.1:mScarlet+ fluorescent intensity (Figure 3B and C), suggesting phagocyte infiltration during p53EPS initiation, prior to typical observation of macroscopic tumor masses (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by neutral red staining and imaging at early time points.

claim: tnfa:EGFP single-positive cells are enriched in her4.1:mScarlet+ lesions.
source: To assess the activation state of phagocytes in and surrounding p53EPS tumors, we co-injected our oncogene combination into tp53-/- embryos carrying a Tg(tnfa:EGFP) transgenic marker of activated and pro-inflammatory phagocytes (Hao et al., 2012; Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015), and observed enrichment of tnfa:EGFP single-positive cells in her4.1:mScarlet+ lesions (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging using a transgenic reporter line.

claim: p53EPS tissues more significantly enrich for gene expression associated with activated and pro-inflammatory phagocytes including classical M1 macrophages, compared to alternative M2 polarized macrophages.
source: However, p53EPS tissues more significantly enriched for gene expression associated with activated and pro-inflammatory phagocytes including classical M1 macrophages, compared to alternative M2 polarized macrophages, and genes typically downregulated during M2 polarization following macrophage colony stimulating factor treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6)
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis against immunologic signature gene sets.

claim: At 5 dpf, comparable levels of mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia are observed throughout the cephalic region and brain in both control and p53EPS-injected zebrafish.
source: At 5 dpf (120 hpf), we observed comparable levels of mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia throughout the cephalic region and in the brain in both control and p53EPS-injected zebrafish (Figure 3F, I).
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging at 5 dpf.

claim: At 7 dpf, small clusters of her4.1:mScarlet+ cells indicative of early lesion formation are surrounded and/or infiltrated by mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia.
source: At 7 dpf, we detected small clusters of her4.1:mScarlet+ cells (Figure 3J, n=5/9), indicative of early lesion formation. Interestingly, these lesions were surrounded and/or infiltrated by mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging at 7 dpf.

claim: At 9 dpf, her4.1:mScarlet+ expression is highly specific to tumor lesions, and these lesions are consistently associated with mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages.
source: while at 9 dpf her4.1:mScarlet+ expression became highly specific to tumor lesions, and these lesions were consistently associated with mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages (Figure 3K, n=8/8 tumor-positive zebrafish).
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging at 9 dpf with quantification.

claim: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages outside of early-stage her4.1:mScarlet+ lesions display highly ramified morphologies with several processes that are extended and retracted.
source: Microglia/macrophages outside of early-stage her4.1:mScarlet+ lesions displayed highly ramified morphologies, with several processes that were extended and retracted, indicative of environmental surveillance (Figure 3L, Video 1; Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging and video microscopy, with comparison to published literature on microglial behavior.

claim: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages infiltrated into dense her4.1:mScarlet+ regions display more rounded and amoeboid-like morphology.
source: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages infiltrated into dense her4.1:mScarlet+ regions displayed more rounded and amoeboid-like morphology, supporting their activation in association with p53EPS oncogenic cells (Karperien et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging observations and comparison to published literature on activated macrophage morphology.

claim: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages in p53EPS oncogenic masses display internalized her4.1:mScarlet+ punctate cells.
source: Interestingly, mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages dynamically interacted with her4.1:mScarlet+ cells (Video 1, Video 2), and in p53EPS oncogenic masses, mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages associated closely with and often displayed internalized her4.1:mScarlet+ punctate cells (Figure 3L and M), suggesting engulfment and removal of p53EPS cells during tumor formation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by live confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Irf7 and Irf8 are upregulated in p53EPS tumor-burdened brains.
source: Interestingly, we observed upregulation of several interferon regulatory factor (Irf) family members including irf7 and irf8 in p53EPS tumor-burdened brains (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression.

claim: irf7 gene targeting efficiency is >90% at 2–5 dpf following CRISPR/Cas9 injection.
source: At 2–5 dpf, we extracted DNA from a subset of injected embryos and observed a gene targeting efficiency of >90% and >65% INDELS at the irf7 or irf8 loci, respectively (ICE Analysis, https://ice.synthego.com/#/, Synthego, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by ICE analysis of CRISPR-targeted genomic DNA.

claim: irf8 gene targeting efficiency is >65% at 2–5 dpf following CRISPR/Cas9 injection.
source: At 2–5 dpf, we extracted DNA from a subset of injected embryos and observed a gene targeting efficiency of >90% and >65% INDELS at the irf7 or irf8 loci, respectively (ICE Analysis, https://ice.synthego.com/#/, Synthego, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by ICE analysis of CRISPR-targeted genomic DNA.

claim: irf8 knock-down results in significant reductions in neutral red-positive phagocytes at 8–10 dpf.
source: Consistent with previous reports, irf8 knock-down resulted in significant reductions in neutral red-positive phagocytes at 8–10 dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Shiau et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by neutral red staining and quantification, consistent with published literature.

claim: 65% of irf7-targeted p53EPS zebrafish develop tumors by 30 dpf.
source: Remarkably, following irf7 or irf8 gene knock-down with p53EPS, we observed robust tumor formation, with 65% of irf7-targeted and 42% of irf8-targeted p53EPS zebrafish developing tumors by 30 dpf, compared to 20% p53EPS incidence (Figure 4A–D, irf7 p<0.0001, irf8 p=0.0155, Fisher's exact test)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative tumor incidence data with statistical analysis.

claim: 42% of irf8-targeted p53EPS zebrafish develop tumors by 30 dpf.
source: Remarkably, following irf7 or irf8 gene knock-down with p53EPS, we observed robust tumor formation, with 65% of irf7-targeted and 42% of irf8-targeted p53EPS zebrafish developing tumors by 30 dpf, compared to 20% p53EPS incidence (Figure 4A–D, irf7 p<0.0001, irf8 p=0.0155, Fisher's exact test)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative tumor incidence data with statistical analysis.

claim: p53EPS tumor brains with irf7 and irf8 knock-down show reduced expression of genes associated with inflammation signature.
source: In p53EPS tumor brains with irf7 and irf8 knock-down, we observed reduced expression of genes associated with our inflammation signature in p53EPS tumor-burdened brains, including immune evasion-associated transcripts like suppressor of cytokine signaling 1a (socs1a) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: irf7 transcript is robustly expressed within early-stage p53EPS lesions at 8 dpf.
source: To further validate gene targeting and assess the spatial localization of irf7 expression within the TME, we performed fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) in control and irf7 knock-down tumors and detected robust transcript expression within early-stage p53EPS lesions at 8 dpf (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization imaging.

claim: Animals co-injected with irf7 CRISPR show reduced irf7 expression in and surrounding tumor cells.
source: In animals co-injected with irf7 CRISPR, we detected p53EPS tumor formation, albeit with reduced irf7 in and surrounding tumor cells (Figure 4E), suggesting potential roles for irf7 in inhibiting p53EPS initiation in tumor cells and/or within the TME.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization imaging and inference about functional roles.

claim: Tumor cell-specific knock-down of irf7 using Tg(her4.1:Cas9-2A-EGFP) does not significantly change p53EPS tumor formation.
source: Despite a gene targeting efficiency of ~28% in pooled tumor cells from five tumor-burdened animals, we did not observe any significant changes in p53EPS tumor formation in Cas9-2A-EGFP-positive zebrafish compared to Cas9-2A-EGFP-negative control-injected siblings (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by tumor incidence data in transgenic animals with tumor cell-specific Cas9 expression.

claim: Tumor cell-specific knock-down of irf8 using Tg(her4.1:Cas9-2A-EGFP) does not significantly change p53EPS tumor formation.
source: We observed similar effects following co-injection of gRNAs targeting irf8 (Figure 4G), suggesting that increased p53EPS tumor initiation following Irf gene knock-down is a consequence of irf7 and irf8 loss-of-function in the TME.
evidence: This is supported by tumor incidence data and inference about the site of action.

claim: 50% of p53EPS tumor cells engraft in host animals co-injected with Clodronate liposomes.
source: At 18 dpt (20 dpf), we observed 50% p53EPS tumor cell engraftment in host animals co-injected with Clodronate liposomes, compared to 23% injected with vehicle control liposomes (p=0.0048, Fisher's exact test, Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments with quantitative engraftment data and statistical analysis.

claim: 23% of p53EPS tumor cells engraft in host animals injected with vehicle control liposomes.
source: At 18 dpt (20 dpf), we observed 50% p53EPS tumor cell engraftment in host animals co-injected with Clodronate liposomes, compared to 23% injected with vehicle control liposomes (p=0.0048, Fisher's exact test, Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments with quantitative engraftment data and statistical analysis.

claim: Co-transplantation with Clodronate liposomes inhibits inflammatory gene expression in bulk tissue.
source: Interestingly, while p53EPS engrafted brains maintained inflammatory gene expression patterns like primary p53EPS tumor-burdened brains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), co-transplantation with Clodronate liposomes inhibited inflammatory gene expression in bulk tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, normalized to mScarlet expression to control for differences in tumor size)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: 46% of p53EPS tumor cells engraft in irf8 CRISPR/Cas9-injected syngeneic host zebrafish at 20 dpf.
source: We also performed p53EPS bulk tumor cell transplantations into the hindbrain ventricles of irf8 CRISPR/Cas9-injected syngeneic host zebrafish embryos at 2 dpf and observed 46% p53EPS tumor cell engraftment at 20 dpf, compared to 19% engraftment in irf8 wild-type host zebrafish (p=0.0002, Fisher's exact test, Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments with quantitative engraftment data and statistical analysis.

claim: 19% of p53EPS tumor cells engraft in irf8 wild-type host zebrafish at 20 dpf.
source: We also performed p53EPS bulk tumor cell transplantations into the hindbrain ventricles of irf8 CRISPR/Cas9-injected syngeneic host zebrafish embryos at 2 dpf and observed 46% p53EPS tumor cell engraftment at 20 dpf, compared to 19% engraftment in irf8 wild-type host zebrafish (p=0.0002, Fisher's exact test, Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments with quantitative engraftment data and statistical analysis.

claim: The innate immune system plays important tumor-suppressive roles during glioblastoma initiation.
source: Altogether, we developed a genetically relevant model of aggressive human glioblastoma and harnessed the unique advantages of zebrafish including live imaging, high-throughput genetic and chemical manipulations to highlight important tumor-suppressive roles for the innate immune system on glioblastoma initiation
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including imaging, gene knockdown, and transplantation experiments.

claim: Tractable vertebrate animal model systems for high-throughput study of tumor development in an intact and endogenous tumor microenvironment remain limited.
source: However, tractable vertebrate animal model systems for high-throughput study of tumor development in an intact and endogenous tumor microenvironment (TME) remain limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on general knowledge.

claim: Therapeutic resistance in glioblastoma can partly be attributed to a poor understanding of underlying molecular mechanisms and significant heterogeneity.
source: Therapeutic resistance can partly be attributed to a poor understanding of underlying molecular mechanisms, as well as a significant level of heterogeneity between patients and within individual tumors.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Recent evidence supports co-existence of inter-converting glioblastoma cell states within individual patient tumors.
source: However, recent evidence supporting co-existence of inter-converting glioblastoma cell states within individual patient tumors reveals less distinct subtype separations and phenotypic flexibilities that contribute to the aggressiveness and drug resistance of glioblastoma across molecular cohorts (Darmanis et al., 2017; Neftel et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2014; Couturier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of PTEN and/or activating mutations in PIK3CA are commonly found in glioblastoma.
source: Loss of the lipid phosphatase PTEN and/or activating mutations in the PI3K catalytic subunit PIK3CA are also commonly found, which altogether drive downstream activation of oncogenic RAS/MAPK and AKT/mTOR signaling, among other crucial pathways involved in growth and survival of glioblastoma (Brennan et al., 2013; McLendon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TP53 loss is implicated in tumor cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and stemness in glioblastoma.
source: Furthermore, the TP53 tumor suppressor pathway is altered in 84% of globlastoma patients and 94% of cell lines, with TP53 loss implicated in tumor cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and stemness (Brennan et al., 2013; McLendon et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The tumor microenvironment in glioblastoma consists of heterogeneous collections of resident brain, stroma, and immune cells, as well as cells recruited from the general circulation.
source: In addition to key genetic drivers, the TME is known to influence cellular flexibility in glioblastoma and consists of heterogeneous collections of resident brain, stroma, and immune cells, as well as cells recruited from the general circulation such as bone marrow-derived immune cells with known tumor-suppressive and tumor-promoting functions (Bikfalvi et al., 2023; Quail and Joyce, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glioblastoma combines a lack of immunogenicity due to few mutations with a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
source: However, like many other tumors, glioblastoma combines a lack of immunogenicity due to few mutations with a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Both tumor and immune cells contribute to immune suppression in and surrounding the TME in glioblastoma.
source: In addition to off-target effects of current frontline therapeutic strategies, both tumor and immune cells contribute to immune suppression in and surrounding the TME in glioblastoma (McGranahan et al., 2019; Sengupta et al., 2012), which could explain the failure of immunotherapy-based clinical trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lymphocytes in glioblastoma are frequently exhausted and dysfunctional.
source: Additionally, lymphocytes are frequently exhausted and dysfunctional and therefore inadequate at exerting an anti-tumor immune response, while tumor-associated myeloid cells are frequently reprogrammed by signaling from tumor cells and the TME to cell states that promote glioblastoma survival, growth, and invasion (Kennedy et al., 2013; McGranahan et al., 2019; Pearson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumor-associated myeloid cells are frequently reprogrammed to cell states that promote glioblastoma survival, growth, and invasion.
source: Additionally, lymphocytes are frequently exhausted and dysfunctional and therefore inadequate at exerting an anti-tumor immune response, while tumor-associated myeloid cells are frequently reprogrammed by signaling from tumor cells and the TME to cell states that promote glioblastoma survival, growth, and invasion (Kennedy et al., 2013; McGranahan et al., 2019; Pearson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumor cells can upregulate myeloid-associated gene expression programs and develop resistance to interferon signaling in response to immune cell attack.
source: Evidence also supports tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms in response to immune cell attack leading to various evasion mechanisms, including upregulation of myeloid-associated gene expression programs and resistance to interferon signaling (Gangoso et al., 2021; Parmigiani et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Roles for the endogenous TME at early stages of tumor initiation remain poorly understood.
source: However, roles for the endogenous TME especially at early stages of tumor initiation, remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge in the field.

claim: Live visualization of heterogeneity and tumor cells within the TME is limited in non-transparent rodent genetic models and/or patient-derived tumor xenografted hosts.
source: Furthermore, live visualization of heterogeneity and tumor cells within the TME is limited in non-transparent rodent genetic models and/or patient-derived tumor xenografted hosts.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of current model systems based on general knowledge.

claim: Irf8 is a conserved determinant of macrophage cell fate and dendritic cell survival and function.
source: Irf8 is a conserved determinant of macrophage cell fate, as well as dendritic cell survival and function, and irf8 mutant zebrafish lack microglia/macrophages in the brain up to 31 dpf (Shiau et al., 2015; Sichien et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: irf8 mutant zebrafish lack microglia/macrophages in the brain up to 31 dpf.
source: Irf8 is a conserved determinant of macrophage cell fate, as well as dendritic cell survival and function, and irf8 mutant zebrafish lack microglia/macrophages in the brain up to 31 dpf (Shiau et al., 2015; Sichien et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Irf7 drives differentiation of macrophages and is broadly activated in immune cells in response to infection.
source: Irf7 also drives differentiation of macrophages; however, in zebrafish and other systems, Irf7 is more broadly activated in immune cells in response to infection, with evidence also supporting non-immune cell-related functions during development and cancer progression (Feng et al., 2016; Gangoso et al., 2021; Günthner and Anders, 2013; Hu et al., 2022; Ning et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most available zebrafish brain tumor models are induced using single oncogenic drivers.
source: However, most of these available zebrafish models are induced using single oncogenic drivers driven by a variety of neuronal and/or glial-specific promoters at different time points throughout development, with the use of single oncogenes in a functional tp53 signaling background potentially contributing to their inability to model highly aggressive and relapse-like phenotypes in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about existing zebrafish models based on review of the literature.

claim: EGFRvIII is a common genetic variant in glioblastoma.
source: One important consideration with model generation is use of genetic drivers that are reflective of variants found in patient tumors. EGFRvIII is a common genetic variant in glioblastoma that we show contributes to aggressive brain tumor formation in our zebrafish model.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field and supported by the experimental use of this variant in the model.

claim: CSF/CSF-1R interactions induce an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype in glioblastoma-associated microglia/macrophages.
source: For example, CSF/CSF-1R interactions have been shown to induce an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype in glioblastoma-associated microglia/macrophages, and blockade of CSF-1R improves survival in tumor-burdened mice (Kennedy et al., 2013; Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Blockade of CSF-1R improves survival in tumor-burdened mice.
source: For example, CSF/CSF-1R interactions have been shown to induce an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype in glioblastoma-associated microglia/macrophages, and blockade of CSF-1R improves survival in tumor-burdened mice (Kennedy et al., 2013; Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Serial transplantation of transformed mouse neural stem cells results in strong negative pressure from the immune system in syngeneic mice.
source: For example, serial transplantation of transformed mouse neural stem cells results in strong negative pressure from the immune system in syngeneic mice, leading to activation of tumor cell-intrinsic immune evasion mechanisms that support growth in vivo and in vitro (Gangoso et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Regions of activated (myeloperoxidase) macrophages in human glioblastoma are associated with improved clinical outcomes.
source: In addition, recent spatial analyses of human glioblastoma tumor samples identified regions of activated (myeloperoxidase) macrophages that are associated with improved clinical outcomes, suggesting anti-tumorigenic roles for certain macrophage populations in patients (Karimi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The transition to mesenchymal-like glioblastoma is closely linked to immune cell infiltration and an immune-suppressive TME.
source: Given that the transition to mesenchymal-like glioblastoma is closely linked to immune cell infiltration and an immune-suppressive TME (Gangoso et al., 2021; Klemm et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The type of glioma affects immune responses, implying that tumor-intrinsic factors shape the composition of the TME.
source: Finally, it is well known that the type of glioma affects immune responses, implying that tumor-intrinsic factors shape the composition of the TME (Friebel et al., 2020; Gangoso et al., 2021; Klemm et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human AKT1 over-expression in zebrafish neural cells drives pre-neoplastic lesions and recruits macrophage and microglia populations through the Sdf1b-Cxcr4b signaling pathway.
source: Human AKT1 over-expression in zebrafish neural cells was previously shown to drive pre-neoplastic lesions in zebrafish larvae and was found to recruit macrophage and microglia populations through the Sdf1b-Cxcr4b signaling pathway (Chia et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In the AKT1-expressing pre-neoplastic neuron model, loss of macrophages resulted in decreased oncogenic proliferation.
source: In this model, loss of macrophages resulted in decreased oncogenic proliferation, suggesting tumor-promoting functions for macrophages at initiation stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a previously published model.

claim: Microglia colonize the zebrafish neural retina by 48 hpf.
source: We first looked at a time-course of lesion formation at 5, 7, and 9 dpf relative to microglia in the zebrafish brain (Figure 3F–K), which colonize the zebrafish neural retina by 48 hpf, and the optic tectum by 84 hpf (Herbomel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.
